body_markdown:
It took about 13 months to turn a waterlogged EV1 from a Georgia tow yard into a running and driving tribute to General Motors engineering history. As we previously reported, Billy Caruso and Jared Pink of *The Questionable Garage* YouTube channel bought a EV1 #212 and announced a partnership with GM to help restore it. The project was onerous and comprehensive, involving everything from dry ice cleaning procuring unobtainium parts from donor cars in GM’s historic collection.[And now it’s done.](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gNlBC6k7Npc&list=PLUK0LPn0iHC_BbTpJcpnz7UYN8ojx8ndL)


From the outside it looks like the duo worked at a whirlwind pace. We[profiled Caruso and Pink](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/general-motors-helps-enthusiasts-restore-a-derelict-ev1/) back in April, when General Motors first went public with the partnership. Pink’s winning bid of $104,000 for the forlorn, derelict EV made a bit more sense given the company’s involvement; the backing of the car’s creators promised to be a boon to the restoration effort.


It also made for a story, and *The Questionable Garag* e went into serious detail documenting the project via regular updates on YouTube. GM donated items like a replacement windshield, and both Caruso and Pink leveraged their working knowledge of the EV1’s older brother, the Chevrolet S-10 EV (1997-98).


Pink and the unrestored EV1.


Questionable Garage | Facebook


Caruso and the restored EV1.


General Motors


Caruso and Pink are now owners of the only running, privately held and road-legal example of GM’s successful but star-crossed 1990s foray into electric propulsion. It started with the Impact concept car in 1990, and over the years we’ve dug[deep into the EV1’s history](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/ev1-may-have-been-first-demise-launched-tesla/) and[even dispelled many myths](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/gm-ev1-true-inside-story/) about it. The project became the subject of a well-known 2006 documentary film called *Who* *Killed the Electric Car?* that lays the blame for the car’s faulure on pressure from oil companies and GM’s fear of lost long-term maintenance revenue. On the other side of the equation was the car’s nascent battery technology, limited range, and high cost.


The end result of the restoration is perhaps even better than when EV1 #212 originally rolled off the assembly line. If nothing else, even if EVs aren’t your cup of tea, this adventure was a labor of love that everyone in this hobby can appreciate.


With just a little over 28,000 miles on its odometer, EV1 #212 has lived a life of innovation, neglect, salvation, and rescue. It’s a singular automobile that can be traced clearly to our current era of electrified vehicles. While Tesla is a household name in America, and Chinese EVs are rapidly hoovering up market share around the world, they all have the GM EV1 to thank for proving the technology had potential.


General Motors


When we spoke to Caruso about #212, he told us he’d probably “drive it up and down Skyline Boulevard (CA-35), and ensure it attends car shows around the country.” So if you’re ever in the San Francisco Bay Area and stumble upon a car meet, keep an eye out. We’d love to see this mean, green little machine slipping through the air on the open road.
